Read a player's list of game scores: all of them, the latest, the best, and the top three.

Adapted from Exercism's [problem specification](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications/tree/main/exercises/high-scores) (MIT). Listed under [Collections & Algorithms](/examples/?subject=collections-and-algorithms).

```nomi-run
// FILE: high_scores.nomi
//# A player's scores in a game, oldest first, and what can be read from
//# them.

/// Every score, oldest first.
pub fn scores(scores: List<Int>) -> List<Int> {
    scores
}

/// The most recent score, or `None` before the first game.
pub fn latest(scores: List<Int>) -> Maybe<Int> {
    Iter.last(scores)
}

/// The highest score, or `None` before the first game.
pub fn personal_best(scores: List<Int>) -> Maybe<Int> {
    Iter.max(scores)
}

/// The three highest scores, highest first, or all of them when there are
/// fewer than three.
pub fn personal_top_three(scores: List<Int>) -> List<Int> {
    scores
    |> Iter.sort(.Descending)
    |> Iter.take(3)
    |> Iter.to_list()
}

// FILE: high_scores_test.nomi
import high_scores

test "List of scores" {
    assert high_scores.scores([30, 50, 20, 70]) == [30, 50, 20, 70]
}

test "Latest score" {
    assert high_scores.latest([100, 0, 90, 30]) == Some(30)
}

test "Personal best" {
    assert high_scores.personal_best([40, 100, 70]) == Some(100)
}

group "Top 3 scores" {
    test "personal top three" {
        cases = [
            #(
                "Personal top three from a list of scores",
                [10, 30, 90, 30, 100, 20, 10, 0, 30, 40, 40, 70, 70],
                [100, 90, 70],
            ),
            #("Personal top highest to lowest", [20, 10, 30], [30, 20, 10]),
            #("Personal top when there is a tie", [40, 20, 40, 30], [40, 40, 30]),
            #("Personal top when there are less than 3", [30, 70], [70, 30]),
            #("Personal top when there is only one", [40], [40]),
        ]

        subtests cases, #(description, scores, expected), description {
            assert high_scores.personal_top_three(scores) == expected
        }
    }

    test "Latest score after personal top scores" {
        scores = [70, 50, 20, 30]
        _ = high_scores.personal_top_three(scores)

        assert high_scores.latest(scores) == Some(30)
    }

    test "Scores after personal top scores" {
        scores = [30, 50, 20, 70]
        _ = high_scores.personal_top_three(scores)

        assert high_scores.scores(scores) == [30, 50, 20, 70]
    }

    test "Latest score after personal best" {
        scores = [20, 70, 15, 25, 30]
        _ = high_scores.personal_best(scores)

        assert high_scores.latest(scores) == Some(30)
    }

    test "Scores after personal best" {
        scores = [20, 70, 15, 25, 30]
        _ = high_scores.personal_best(scores)

        assert high_scores.scores(scores) == [20, 70, 15, 25, 30]
    }
}
```

## How it's written

- The scores are a plain `List<Int>`, oldest first, and each property is a file-level function over it. A `HighScores` struct wrapping one list would add a constructor and a field read and nothing else. `scores` answers the list it is given, kept because the canonical data names the property.
- `latest` and `personal_best` answer `Maybe<Int>`, since a player who has not played has neither; they are `Iter.last` and `Iter.max`. The canonical lists are never empty, so the tests assert `Some(...)`.
- `personal_top_three` is `Iter.sort(.Descending)`, `Iter.take(3)` and `Iter.to_list`, which keeps ties and answers fewer than three when there are fewer.
- The four "after" cases check that reading the top three or the best leaves the scores as they were. Values are immutable, so they hold by construction; the tests still call the reader first and then check, as the canonical cases describe.
- The canonical "Top 3 scores" group is a `group` of that name. Its five `personalTopThree` rows are one `subtests` table, and the four "after" cases are tests of their own, since each checks a different reader.
